name: Neelakandeswarar Temple, Rajendrapattinam (Thiru Erukkathampuliyur)
deity: Shiva as Neelakandeswarar (Swetharanyeswarar, Thirukumaresar), with the goddess Neelamalarkanni
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu near Vriddhachalam, sung by Sambandar in the Tevaram (7th century); birthplace of Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar
dynasty: Chola, associated with Rajaraja I and Rajendra I
summary: At Rajendrapattinam, the Erukkathampuliyur of the Tevaram, Shiva is worshipped as Neelakandeswarar in the home village of Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar, whose yazh once carried Sambandar's hymns.

sections.history: Rajendrapattinam is a village of Cuddalore district, a little south of Vriddhachalam off the road to Jayankondam, and its Shiva temple is the Thiru Erukkathampuliyur of the Tevaram. It is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams, counted among the shrines of Nadu Nadu, and Thirugnana Sambandar sang it. The village holds a special place in that saint's story, for it was the birthplace of Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar, the Nayanar who travelled with Sambandar and played the yazh, the old Tamil harp, as the child-saint sang. The stone temple is a Chola work, and local tradition links it with Rajaraja I and his son Rajendra I, from whom the village takes its present name.
sections.architecture: The temple is a Chola-period stone shrine in the Dravidian manner, set in a walled enclosure with the sanctum of the lingam and a separate shrine for the goddess Neelamalarkanni, whose name means she of the blue-lotus eyes. In front lies the temple tank, the Neelotpala theertham, named for the blue water lily. A shrine honours Thiruneelakanda Yazhpanar, with images of the musician-saint and his wife, keeping the village's own Nayanar close to the Lord he served with music.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that Murugan, after a quarrel with his father, was cursed to be born on earth as a mute boy. He went from shrine to shrine, and here at last his speech returned; he is said to have struck his vel into the ground to bring forth the tank before the temple. So Shiva is also called Thirukumaresar, the Lord who freed Kumara. The old name Erukkathampuliyur recalls the erukku, the white arka plant, and tradition adds that Rajaraja Chola prayed here for a son and was blessed with Rajendra.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva year of the region: monthly Pradosham, Maha Shivaratri in Masi, Arudra Darshanam in Margazhi, and the Navaratri days of the goddess, with Skanda Shashti honouring Murugan, whose story is woven into the shrine. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Rajendrapattinam is a quiet village temple where the music of the Tevaram feels close at hand. Stand before the shrine of Yazhpanar and remember the harp that accompanied Sambandar's hymns, look out over the blue-lily tank, and worship the Lord who gave Murugan back his voice. It pairs naturally with the great Vriddhagireeswarar temple at Vriddhachalam nearby.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples of the region. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Rajendrapattinam lies about 13 km from Vriddhachalam, just off the Vriddhachalam–Jayankondam road; buses and hired autos run from Vriddhachalam. Vriddhachalam Junction is the nearest railway station; Tiruchirappalli and Puducherry are the nearest airports.
